instagram_reel.hook: Sangiovese is not one wine — it’s a whole family of Italian personalities.
instagram_reel.script:
If Sangiovese has ever made you feel a little lost on a wine list, you are not alone. 

Here’s the easy version: it’s Italy’s most planted red grape, and it shows up under different names depending on where it’s grown. Chianti, Brunello di Montalcino, Vino Nobile di Montepulciano — same grape, different style.

What should you expect? Tart cherry, red plum, dried herbs, and that bright acidity that makes your mouth water.

And that acidity is exactly why Sangiovese is such a great food wine. Tomato sauce, pizza, pasta — it just works.

So the next time you see Sangiovese on a label, don’t panic. Think: Italian red, high acid, made for the table.

Chianti? Sangiovese. Brunello di Montalcino? Also Sangiovese. Vino Nobile di Montepulciano? Yep, Sangiovese again.

What do you get in the glass? Usually tart cherry, red plum, dried herbs, and really bright acidity.

linkedin.post:
Sangiovese is one of the clearest examples of why wine education should feel approachable, not intimidating.

It is Italy’s most planted red grape, but many drinkers know it better through the regional names on the label: Chianti, Brunello di Montalcino, and Vino Nobile di Montepulciano. Once you understand that those wines are all expressions of the same grape, the Italian section of the shelf gets a lot easier to navigate.

What makes Sangiovese so compelling is range. It can show tart cherry and red plum in one style, then deeper structure, firmer tannin, and more age-worthiness in another. It is also defined by high acidity, which is exactly why it pairs so naturally with tomato-based dishes and other food-forward meals.

From an industry perspective, Sangiovese is also a useful reminder that regional naming conventions can either confuse or invite. When we explain them well, we help more people feel confident choosing wine — and that confidence is what keeps them engaged.

That is the kind of wine story I always want to tell: clear, useful, and grounded in the glass.
